notes:
I could only read some of the sites on your list. The pages I used were Enduring Word (Guzik), the Bible Hub and StudyLight commentary pages (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Barnes, Calvin, Benson, Henry, Poole, Clarke, Keil‑Delitzsch, Cambridge, Constable, Chuck Smith), Blue Letter Bible (Henry), and the NET Bible note on v. 15. I found nothing on the Catholic, Orthodox or Lutheran sites, and nothing on prosperity or hyper‑grace teaching, so those are left out. Benson and Clarke stand in for the Methodist side, Calvin and Henry for the Reformed side, and Gill for the Baptist side.

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Guzik takes the context to be God's promise in ch. 31 that Assyria would be judged. God didn't want only to remove the threat; He also wanted to bless Judah with a righteous king. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-32/
- Hezekiah partly fulfilled it, yet ultimately, Hezekiah was a picture of the King of Kings, Jesus Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-32/
- Guzik says the "princes" are Jesus' people (1 Pet 2:9; Rev 5:10). In his view, trials train believers to rule with Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-32/
- Ellicott translates it "the king". He reads vv. 1–8 as a separate picture of the ideal king, like Isaiah 11, not, of course without a reference to the character of Hezekiah as the partial and present embodiment of the idea. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/32-1.htm
- Calvin explains the terms: "righteousness" means fair and good government, and "judgment" means protecting good people from the wicked. A good king also needs good officials, who shall supply the place of eyes and hands. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/32.htm

**v. 2**
- Benson says "a man" means the king or each of his princes. They protect people who are oppressed by the powerful, and the "weary land" is a scorched land that wears travellers out. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/isaiah-32.html
- Guzik says Jesus' reign is all of these things for us: shelter, rivers and shade. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-32/

**vv. 3–4**
- Benson: the people will no longer close their eyes and ears to good advice. The "rash" are people who judge too quickly. The "stammerers" used to speak about God vaguely and reluctantly. He says this was only partly fulfilled under Hezekiah and fully in Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/isaiah-32.html
- Guzik links it to the renewal under Hezekiah. He also suggests God would bless in miraculous ways with the stammering tongue speaking clearly. (Note: this quote is actually from Clarke, quoted on that page.) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-32/

**v. 5**
- The Hebrew word for "fool" is *nabal*. Pulpit and Cambridge compare Nabal in 1 Samuel 25. Pulpit says people tend to call wasteful party‑givers "generous" and hoarders "well‑off", and This perversion of truth shall not obtain in Messiah's kingdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/32-5.htm
- Cambridge says the word translated "scoundrel" (KJV "churl") appears only here and in v. 7, and its meaning is uncertain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/32-5.htm
- Ellicott sees this as the reverse of Isaiah 5:20, where people "called good evil, and evil good". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/32-5.htm

**vv. 6–7**
- Benson: the fool does wrong behind a show of religion, gives unjust verdicts, and takes food and drink from the poor. The "weapons" of the scoundrel can include the corrupt people he hires to carry out his plans. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/isaiah-32.html
- Guzik quotes Motyer: the word for "plots" usually has a bad meaning and describes planning for your own gain whatever it costs others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-32/

**v. 8**
- Benson: the generous person is not ruined by being generous, as wicked people imagine. His generosity makes him secure. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/isaiah-32.html
- Henry: Charity must be directed by wisdom, so that it is not wasted. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/32-5.html

**v. 9**
- Pulpit says the Hebrew word for "at ease" is almost always used in a bad sense. It pictures the women lounging on couches and being told to stand up for a word from God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/32-9.htm
- Calvin says Isaiah speaks to women to show how wide the disaster will be: women are usually spared in war, but this time no one will be. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/32-9.html
- Guzik, quoting Wolf, points out that the words for "at ease" and "complacent" come back in v. 18 as God's promised secure, peaceful dwellings. Security is good when it rests on the Lord. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-32/
- Gill says some take "daughters" to mean the villages, following Ben Melech. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/reb/isaiah/32-9.html

**v. 10**
- Benson reads "a year and some days" as the length of the Assyrian invasion. He works it out from Hezekiah's reign: the invasion came in his fourteenth year, and God then added fifteen more years. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/isaiah-32.html

**v. 11**
- Benson: they are to take off their ornaments (compare Exodus 33:5) and put on sackcloth like mourners and penitents. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/isaiah-32.html

**vv. 12–14**
- Benson, quoting Lowth: the Assyrian siege was only a foretaste. This desolation must, at least, extend to the ruin of the country and city by the Chaldeans. (Note: this cited text is actually from a StudyLight result and says something slightly different. Lowth's own words are on Benson's page.) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/isaiah-32.html
- Guzik: God would use hard economic times to wake Judah up, and those times would reach everyone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-32/
- Coffman: v. 15 shows that "forever" in v. 14 has a limit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/32-15.html

**v. 15**
- Pulpit: "until" qualifies "forever", and the desert‑to‑orchard‑to‑forest sequence is a deliberate climax. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/32-15.htm
- Ellicott: Isaiah here follows Joel in looking for a Spirit outpouring that would sweep away decadent luxury. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/32-15.htm
- Guzik: the hard times last until the Spirit comes. The Spirit is poured out, not sprinkled, and comes from heaven, not from human effort. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-32/
- Calvin hears an echo of Psalm 104:30. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/32-15.html

**vv. 16–17**
- Clarke: Righteousness works and produces peace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/isaiah/32.htm
- Benson: the result is peace of conscience and peace with God, or possibly outward prosperity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/isaiah-32.html
- Henry: Christ's law gives the rule we must live by, and his gospel gives the righteousness by which we are saved. Both last wherever the Spirit is poured out. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_032.cfm
- Guzik: we should not be satisfied with anything claiming to be from the Spirit that lacks the fruit of the Spirit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-32/

**v. 18**
- Benson: "my people" means the converted Gentiles, or the Jews when they turn to Christ in the last days. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/isaiah-32.html
- Guzik: those blessed by the Spirit live above their circumstances. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-32/

**v. 19** (see the section on differences below)
- Clarke admits the verse is very obscure. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/32-19.html
- Barnes says there is a wordplay in the Hebrew, and hail stands for God's punishment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/32-19.html

**v. 20**
- Keil‑Delitzsch reads it literally: people will sow wherever they like and let their animals roam without worry. There cannot be the slightest doubt that this is the correct explanation, comparing Isaiah 30:23–25. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/32-20.htm
- Barnes and Clarke, following Chardin, describe the Eastern way of sowing rice: seed is scattered on flooded ground and oxen and donkeys trample the mud. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/isaiah/32-20.html
- Pulpit: A spiritual meaning doubtless underlies the literal sense. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/32-20.htm

## Where traditions differ

**v. 1: Who is the king?**
- Barnes says flatly that the king is Hezekiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/32-1.html
- Calvin (Reformed) says it is Hezekiah, but because the Church cannot flourish without Christ, it undoubtedly refers to Christ, of whom Hezekiah was a type. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/32.htm
- Benson (Methodist) agrees it is Hezekiah as a type of Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/isaiah-32.html
- Gill (Baptist) mostly sets Hezekiah aside, allowing him at most as a type. He reads it rather Christ himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/32-1.htm
- Guzik also mentions that some think the king could be Josiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-32/

**v. 15: When is the Spirit poured out?**
- Benson (Methodist) and Poole say it happened in part at the return from Babylon, and far more fully at Pentecost on the apostles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/32-15.htm
- Henry says The kingdom of the Messiah was brought in, and set up, by the pouring out of the Spirit (Acts 2:1-13). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/32-15.html
- Gill (Baptist) says it cannot mean Pentecost. It points to an outpouring still to come, which will bring in the full number of the Gentiles and the conversion of the Jews. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/32-15.htm
- Barnes argues that "until" limits the verse, at the utmost, to the return from Babylon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/32-15.htm
- Benson and some cited by Henry read the wilderness and forest as an allegory: the Gentiles converted and the Jews rejected. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/isaiah-32.html
- The Bible Hub study note takes a dispensational view: a future national outpouring on Israel and literal fruitfulness of the land, with Pentecost as a first taste. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/32-15.htm
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) connects it to the modern state of Israel draining marshes and farming the land, and to a final outpouring like Joel's. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/32-19.html

**v. 19: What are the forest and the city?**
- Barnes: the forest is the Assyrian army and the city is Nineveh or Babylon. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/32-19.html
- Gill: the forest is the Antichrist and his states, and the city is "mystical Babylon", meaning Rome. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/32-19.html
- Calvin: God turns storms away from his people onto others. The low‑lying city is safe without walls because God protects it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/32-19.html
- Constable: a near and a far meaning blend here, the Assyrians soon and the fallen world later. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/32-19.html
- Coffman: the city is the great world‑city of Revelation 16:19. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/32-19.html

**v. 20: Literal or spiritual sowing?**
- Gill says these words are directed to the ministers of the Gospel in the latter day. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/32-20.html
- Henry says some apply it to the apostles' preaching, and he also applies it to acts of charity. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_032.cfm
- Jamieson‑Fausset‑Brown mention Castalio's idea that the ox and donkey allude to the Jew–Gentile distinction, which the gospel removes, but reject it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/32-20.htm

**Millennial readings**
- Constable notes that Many amillennial interpreters take the eschatological blessings of the chapter as Christ's eternal heavenly reign. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/32-20.html
- Benson relates vv. 15–20 to the gospel church in the apostolic and millennial periods. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/isaiah-32.html

## Other views

**Modern scholarship**
- The NET Bible translates v. 15 as "new life is poured out on us". Its note explains that the Hebrew literally says "a spirit is emptied out", that the verb usually means "lay bare", and that *ruakh* is often but not always taken as God's Spirit. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Isa&chapter=32&verse=15
- The Cambridge Bible suggests the closing farm scene may partly reflect Isaiah's own love of farming. It contrasts that scene with the false sophistication and military display that will be swept away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/32-20.htm

**Debated popular teaching**
- Chuck Smith reads vv. 5–6 as describing theological "liberals". I found this only in his own commentary; the other commentators read "liberal" in the old sense of "noble" or "generous". https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/32-19.html
